name: Glaetzer Shiraz Amon-Ra Barossa Valley 2010
text:
## Glaetzer Shiraz Amon-Ra Barossa Valley 2010

**The story.** The first Glaetzers came to the [Barossa Valley](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Barossa+Valley,+South+Australia,+Australia&t=k) in 1888, emigrating from [Brandenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg) in Germany. They sailed on the [Norddeutscher Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norddeutscher_Lloyd) steamer *Habsburg*, took seven weeks to reach [Port Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Adelaide), and settled in the country town of [Nuriootpa](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Nuriootpa,+South+Australia,+Australia&t=k), becoming some of the earliest recorded grape growers in the Barossa and [Clare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare_Valley) valleys ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/the-glaetzer-family/)). They were following a well-worn path: the Barossa's wine industry was founded by German settlers fleeing persecution in [Silesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silesia), which is why it feels so unlike the British-shaped rest of Australian wine ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).

A century later, Colin Glaetzer, who studied agriculture and oenology at [Roseworthy College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseworthy_College), ran Barossa Valley Estate from 1985, where he created the E&E Black Pepper Shiraz. In 1995 he, his wife Judith and their three sons founded Glaetzer Wines, with a first vintage in 1996 ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/colin-glaetzer/)). His son Ben, who studied winemaking at the [University of Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Adelaide), now makes the wines. His honours include Qantas Young Winemaker of the Year and Robert Parker's Wine Personality of the Year, and both father and son are "Barons of the Barossa" for their contribution to the valley's culture ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/ben-glaetzer/)).

**The vineyards.** Every grape comes from one small corner of the northern Barossa, [Ebenezer](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ebenezer,+South+Australia,+Australia&t=k) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebenezer,_South_Australia)). The finest fruit is from dry-grown, ungrafted [bush vines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vine_training) 80 to 110 years old, the oldest yielding only half a tonne to a tonne per acre, tended by third and fourth-generation growers. Ebenezer is warmer and drier than the southern Barossa, and its well-drained sandy clay loam over a solid [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone) pan is "mean" soil that sends roots deep and gives concentrated wines ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/the-vineyards/)). The Barossa is famous for these old vines: some are 100 to 150 years old, and Turkey Flat in [Tanunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanunda,_South_Australia) has vines planted in 1847, described as the oldest commercially producing grapevines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).

**The winemaking.** Ben ferments in small one- and two-tonne open fermenters, plunged by hand three times a day, with long time on skins for softness and tannin. The wine goes through [malolactic fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malolactic_fermentation) in [hogshead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogshead) barrels and matures 12 to 18 months ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/the-winemaking/)). The top wines are bottled unfiltered.

**The wine: Amon-Ra.** Amon-Ra is the Glaetzer flagship Shiraz ([Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah)), below only the rare Eye of Ra. The name comes from Egyptian mythology: [Amun-Ra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amun) was considered the king of all gods, and the estate says his temple was believed to be the first to plant a single-variety vineyard to make wine for its people. The eye on the label is the [Eye of Horus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_of_Horus), or wedjat ("whole one"), an Egyptian symbol of protection drawn in six parts, which the Egyptians matched to six senses: touch, taste, hearing, sight, smell and thought. Ben made Amon-Ra to appeal to all six ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/amon-ra/)).

It is always 100% Shiraz from Ebenezer vines 50 to 130 years old, yielding about 2 tonnes per hectare, fermented in small open vats, then matured 16 months on its lees in 100% new oak hogsheads (95% French, 5% American) and bottled unfiltered. In 2018 Amon-Ra was included in the seventh edition of [Langton's Classification of Australian Wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langton's_Classification_of_Australian_Wine), the auction house's ranking of the country's most sought-after wines ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Amon-Ra-Langtons-7th-Edition.pdf)).

The style has changed over time. Matthew Jukes writes that Ben admits the early vintages "were supposed to shock international wine commentators with their scale and impact", and that he has since gradually reined the wine in, adding finesse and detail ([Glaetzer, 2016 press reviews](https://glaetzer.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/2016-amon-ra-Press-Review.pdf)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [South Australia vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/south-australia) calls 2010 "the year that the rain finally came", breaking a long drought. Too much rain later in the season brought some mildew, but overall the impression across South Australia is positive. For dry-grown old vines like Glaetzer's, a winter of good rain after years of drought was a welcome reset.

**What the critics say for 2010.**
- **[James Halliday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Halliday_%28writer%29): 95** (November 2011, as quoted by [Cellarit](https://www.cellarit.com.au/wine-65893-glaetzer-amon-ra-shiraz-2010.aspx)). Impenetrable in colour, with a mélange of black fruits, oak, spice, tar and licorice; the palate reveals "even more dark fruits, more depth, in fact, more of everything, and that is the essence of the wine". "This will go the distance", and if you like impressive wines, "search no further". Drink to 2050.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.2** (from your CellarTracker list).
- (Retail listings also quote Robert Parker and Wine Spectator scores for the 2010, but on pages I couldn't open, so I've left them out.)

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is sixteen years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2020 to 2027, while Halliday said drink to 2050. The truth for most bottles is probably in between: at sixteen, an early-era Amon-Ra built on scale should have softened into dark fruit, licorice, tar, leather and spice, with the new oak absorbed. I'd open it within the next few years. Stand it up a day ahead and decant it off its sediment for an hour or two.

**Serving.** These are big, unfiltered wines, so stand the bottle up a day ahead and [decant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) it, both to leave the sediment behind and to give it air: an hour or two for older bottles, longer for young ones. One critic suggests drinking a young bottle over a couple of days, as the coffee and chocolate notes "melt down and harmonize" ([Glaetzer, 2018 Amon-Ra press reviews](https://glaetzer.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/2018-amon-ra-Press-Review.pdf)). Serve at about 16 to 18°C; too warm, and the alcohol shows.

**Food.** This is a wine for rich, robust food. My picks: a thick, charred [rib eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_eye_steak) or [wagyu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagyu), slow-roasted lamb shoulder or braised [lamb shanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shank_%28meat%29), barbecued beef brisket, or, in honour of the Barossa's German roots, a smoky [mettwurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mettwurst) with sauerkraut. Strong, hard aged cheeses work too. I'd avoid delicate fish and very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists Amon-Ra or Anaperenna at the moment, but BC Liquor carries Glaetzer's ultra-premium Shiraz, The Eye of Ra, at $600. Back vintages of Amon-Ra turn up with Australian merchants and at auction; it is far less expensive than Australia's most famous icon Shiraz, [Penfolds Grange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penfolds_Grange).

**From the history books**
- **A misspelled valley.** Colonel [William Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Light) named the valley in 1837 after the [Battle of Barrosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Barrosa) in Spain, where he had fought in 1811; a clerical error registered it as "Barossa" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).
- **Three ships to Silesia.** In 1841 the South Australian Company chartered three ships to Silesia offering refuge and land to settlers; nearly 500 families came, and found the warm valley ideal for vines, though Silesia had almost no winemaking tradition ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).
- **From port to Shiraz.** For decades the Barossa made mainly fortified "port-style" wines, and in the mid-20th century it was seen as an inferior region, with its old Shiraz vines used in anonymous blends. In the 1980s, small family producers of old-vine Shiraz won international acclaim, and Jancis Robinson came to call the Barossa "Australia's quintessential wine region" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).
- **Protected by law.** To stop the valley turning into a suburb of [Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide), South Australia passed the Character Preservation (Barossa Valley) Act in 2012 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barossa_Valley_wine_region)).

**Curious details**
- **No cellar door.** Glaetzer has no cellar door: there is nowhere to drop in and taste ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/amon-ra/)).
- **A seven-week voyage.** The family's 1888 crossing from Germany to Port Adelaide on the *Habsburg* took seven weeks ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/the-glaetzer-family/)).
- **Winemakers galore.** The estate says the founding of Glaetzer Wines began "a new era" for a family that "boasts more than its fair share of winemakers" ([Glaetzer Wines](https://glaetzer.com/the-glaetzer-family/)).
